Threat.value: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

vignette:
The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, after a fourteen-hour day. Margaret had just left the courthouse, her briefcase heavy with files for a sentencing hearing the next morning, when a man came up behind her in the parking garage. She never heard his footsteps. She only felt his arm lock around her throat and the cold press of metal against her temple. He took her wallet, her phone, her car keys, and then he shoved her face-first into the concrete pillar before running. She lay there for what felt like an hour, though it was probably only minutes, until a security guard found her. She was seventy-six at the time, still working full-time as a public defender, still believing she could handle anything the job threw at her.

In the weeks afterward, Margaret tried to keep going. She went back to work after three days, because the sentencing hearing couldn't wait and because she had always prided herself on being tougher than the circumstances. But something had shifted. She began to notice that she could not walk through the courthouse lobby without scanning every face, without cataloguing the hands of every man she passed. She found herself watching people’s eyes, their postures, the way they held their shoulders. She was certain that if she looked closely enough, she could spot the ones who meant harm before they acted. She had come to believe that the attack had happened because she had not been paying attention, because she had been too tired, too distracted, too old to see it coming. And she was not going to make that mistake again.

The checking started gradually. At first it was just a glance over her shoulder when she heard footsteps behind her on the sidewalk. Then it became a habit: every few steps, a quick turn of the head, a scan of the pavement behind her. She did it so often that her neck began to ache by the end of the day. She started to avoid the parking garage altogether, arriving at work an hour early to find street parking three blocks away, even though it meant walking through a different part of the city. She told herself it was safer, that the street had more people, more witnesses. But the walk itself became a ritual of vigilance. She would count the number of people ahead of her, behind her, across the street. She would cross to the other side if a man was walking in her direction. She began to feel her heart race at the sound of a car door slamming, at the sudden bark of a dog, at any unexpected noise that came from behind her.

Her husband, Robert, noticed the changes. She had stopped agreeing to their evening walks around the neighborhood, claiming her knees were bothering her. She no longer wanted to go to the grocery store after dark. At dinner, she would startle if he came up behind her to refill her water glass. She would flinch, drop her fork, and then apologize, embarrassed. He asked her once if she wanted to talk about what happened, and she said no, that she was fine, that it was just her nerves, that she would get over it. But she did not get over it. The startle response only grew worse. A car backfiring on the street outside their apartment sent her heart pounding for twenty minutes. A knock on the door made her freeze in the kitchen, waiting, listening, until Robert answered it.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was not the fear itself, but the accumulation of its consequences. She had been assigned a new case—a young man charged with armed robbery—and she found herself unable to read the police report without her hands shaking. She could not look at the defendant without imagining his hands around her throat. She had to ask for a continuance, something she had never done in forty-two years of practice. Her supervisor suggested she take some time off. Margaret heard the suggestion as a verdict: she was no longer capable. She made an appointment with a therapist the next day. She is not sure what she hopes for, exactly. She knows she cannot keep looking over her shoulder forever. But what frightens her most is the possibility that the vigilance is the only thing keeping her safe, and that if she stops, she will be caught off guard again.
